The Bill of Rights. The first ten amendments to the United States Constitution, ratified in seventeen ninety-one, the Bill of Rights was drafted primarily by James Madison in response to Anti-Federalist demands for explicit protections of individual liberties. It enshrines fundamental freedoms—speech, religion, press, assembly, petition, due process, and jury trial—that define American civil rights and remain the foundation of constitutional law governing personal freedoms.

James Madison initially opposed a bill of rights, arguing that the Constitution's structure and enumerated powers already protected liberty. He changed his mind under political pressure from Thomas Jefferson and Anti-Federalists who feared unchecked federal power. The First Amendment protects freedoms of religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition. It is the most litigated amendment and the foundation of American free speech doctrine.

The Second Amendment protects the right to bear arms. Its interpretation—whether it protects an individual right or a collective right tied to militia service—remains hotly contested in contemporary gun-control debates. The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures, establishing the foundation for privacy rights and requiring warrants based on probable cause. It has spawned vast jurisprudence on wiretapping, digital privacy, and police conduct.

The Fifth Amendment provides due process protections, protections against self-incrimination, and guarantees against double jeopardy. The phrase "taking the Fifth" enters popular speech through this amendment. The Sixth Amendment guarantees the right to counsel, speedy trial, and confrontation of witnesses. The Seventh Amendment preserves jury trial in civil cases. The Eighth Amendment prohibits cruel and unusual punishment. The Ninth and Tenth Amendments reserve rights and powers to the people and states respectively. Later, the Fourteenth Amendment incorporated most Bill of Rights protections against the states.
